description:
## What breaks

Calling a guard helper with a literal argument aborts the interpreter and works on the other two doors.

```
fn gt?(lo, x), do: x > lo
fn kind(x) when gt?(0, x), do: :pos
fn kind(_x), do: :neg
fn main() do
  dbg(kind(5))
  dbg(kind(-5))
end
```

- `fz2 interp` -> `fz2 interp: backend clause dispatch required omitted semantic input 1` (a bare string, no diagnostic, no span)
- `fz2 run` -> `:pos` / `:neg`
- `fz2 build` -> `:pos` / `:neg`

Replacing the literal with a parameter makes interp agree:

```
fn between?(lo, hi, x), do: x >= lo and x <= hi
fn kind(lo, hi, x) when between?(lo, hi, x), do: :in   # works on all three doors
```

## Why

`guard_dispatch_from_surface` (src/dispatch_matrix/pattern.rs) allocates a `PatternPinnedInput` for each guard-call argument that is not a clause parameter. Those pinned slots land in `dispatch.required_input_ordinals()` as ordinals past the function's real arity: `kind/1` has semantic input 0 (its parameter) plus pinned ordinal 1 (the literal `0`). With two literals -- `when between?(1, 10, x)` -- interp reports ordinal 2, matching pinned ordinals 1 and 2 exactly.

Both backends check the same predicate, but from different input vectors:

- src/compiler2/jobs/native.rs:871 builds its vector with `bind_executable_inputs`, which carries the pinned slots, so the check passes.
- src/ir_interp/backend.rs:609 (`select_clause`) checks the caller's `args`, which only ever holds the real arguments, so any pinned ordinal is `None` and the call aborts.

One question -- "what are this dispatch's semantic inputs?" -- with two implementations that disagree. See .agent/docs/semantic-authorities.md.

## Acceptance

- A fixture with a literal-argument guard helper produces identical output on interp, run and build.
- The interpreter obtains pinned inputs from the same authority the native lowerer uses, rather than from the call's argument list.
- If a required input is genuinely absent it surfaces as a diagnostic with a span, not as a bare backend string.
title: [BUG] A literal argument to a guard helper becomes a pinned semantic input that the interpreter never supplies
